courses.title: Materials & making
courses.description: A closer look at the things we build with.
courses.hero: From tiny structures to big ideas.

units.title: Start with the structure
units.description: Atoms, bonds, and the patterns between them.

lesson.heading: Structure comes first
lesson.body: A material’s structure describes how its parts are arranged. Start with a small repeating pattern, then ask how that pattern shapes the object you can hold.
lesson.example: Compare a neat stack of blocks with a loose pile. Both use the same blocks, but their arrangements change how they respond to a push.
lesson.activity: Sketch a repeating pattern. Identify one unit that can be repeated to reconstruct the whole sketch.

questions.prompt: What does a repeating unit describe?
options: A pattern that builds the larger structure
The weight of the entire object
questions.explanation: A repeating unit is a small pattern that can reconstruct a larger arrangement.
questions.hint: Look for the option that matches the main idea of the lesson.

questions.prompt: A sample has a mass of 12 g and a volume of 4 cm³. What is its density?
questions.explanation: Density is mass divided by volume: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 g/cm³.
questions.hint: Write the relationship first, then substitute the values and keep the units.

lesson.heading: Put a number on it
lesson.body: A measurement connects an observation to a number and a unit. A useful record includes what you measured, how you measured it, and what could change the result.
lesson.example: Imagine comparing two strips by bending them with the same load. Keep the strip dimensions and the loading method consistent so the comparison is useful.
lesson.activity: Write a measurement plan. Name the quantity, its unit, and one condition you would keep fixed.
lesson.formula: mean = sum of values / number of values

questions.prompt: What belongs beside every measured value?
questions.explanation: A unit tells the reader what scale and quantity the number represents.
questions.hint: Look for the option that matches the main idea of the lesson.

questions.prompt: Three measurements are 2, 4, and 6 mm. What is their mean?
questions.explanation: Add the three values and divide by three: (2 + 4 + 6) ÷ 3 = 4 mm.
questions.hint: Write the relationship first, then substitute the values and keep the units.

lesson.heading: One change at a time
lesson.body: A small experiment starts with a question you can test. Choose an input to change, an output to measure, and conditions to keep the same.
lesson.example: Make two paper beams with different folds. Compare them using the same paper, span, and load. Record the differences before drawing a conclusion.
lesson.activity: Propose one experiment. State your question and choose the one variable you will change.
lesson.formula: total time = trials × time per trial

questions.prompt: Which comparison is easiest to interpret?
questions.explanation: Changing one variable helps connect the observed result to that change.
questions.hint: Look for the option that matches the main idea of the lesson.

questions.prompt: A process takes 10 minutes per trial. How long do three trials take?
questions.explanation: Three trials × 10 minutes per trial = 30 minutes.
questions.hint: Write the relationship first, then substitute the values and keep the units.

units.title: Build something of your own
units.description: An open-ended project, from question to reflection.

lesson.heading: Bring an idea to life
lesson.body: A good first project can be small. Choose a question, make a simple version, and decide what evidence would show whether it works.
lesson.example: Use a project notebook to record choices and unexpected results. A useful reflection explains what you tried and what you would change next.
lesson.activity: Draft a project brief with a goal, a first experiment, and one way to check success.

assignment.title: Practice 04: build something of your own

questions.prompt: What makes a project goal useful?
questions.explanation: A goal that can be checked gives you a way to judge your next step.
questions.hint: Look for the option that matches the main idea of the lesson.

questions.prompt: You finish 3 of 4 project tasks. What percentage is complete?
questions.hint: Write the relationship first, then substitute the values and keep the units.

courses.title: Circuits & signals
courses.description: A space to explore electronics, one connection at a time.
courses.hero: Follow a signal. Find an idea.

units.title: Meet the circuit
units.description: Nodes, loops, and a first simple model.

lesson.heading: A circuit is a set of connections
lesson.body: A circuit model describes components and the connections between them. Begin by labeling the nodes, then identify which components connect each pair.
lesson.example: Draw one source and one resistor in a closed loop. Label the source voltage and choose a current direction before you calculate.
lesson.activity: Draw a simple loop. Label each component and the current direction you choose.

questions.prompt: What does a node represent?
questions.explanation: A node represents points joined by ideal wire in a circuit model.
questions.hint: Look for the option that matches the main idea of the lesson.

questions.prompt: A 10 V source is connected across a 5 Ω resistor. What is the current?
questions.explanation: Ohm’s law gives I = V/R = 10/5 = 2 A.
questions.hint: Write the relationship first, then substitute the values and keep the units.

lesson.heading: Write down the relationship
lesson.body: A resistor model relates the voltage across the component to the current through it. Use consistent reference directions when writing the relationship.
lesson.example: Two equal resistors in series carry the same current. Their voltage drops add to the total applied voltage.
lesson.activity: Sketch two resistors in series. Mark a current direction and each voltage drop.

questions.prompt: Which quantity is equal through series components?
questions.explanation: Components in a single series path carry the same current.
questions.hint: Look for the option that matches the main idea of the lesson.

questions.prompt: What is the total resistance of 3 Ω and 7 Ω resistors in series?
questions.explanation: Series resistances add: 3 + 7 = 10 Ω.
questions.hint: Write the relationship first, then substitute the values and keep the units.

units.title: Look at a changing signal
units.description: Time, period, and the shape of a waveform.

lesson.heading: Read the time axis
lesson.body: A periodic signal repeats after one period. Frequency counts how many cycles occur per second. Keep the units visible when you convert between them.
lesson.example: Sketch a repeating wave and mark two neighboring peaks. The time between equivalent points is one period.
lesson.activity: Sketch a periodic signal. Label one complete cycle and its period.

assignment.title: Practice 03: look at a changing signal

questions.prompt: What does frequency count?
questions.explanation: Frequency counts cycles per second, measured in hertz.
questions.hint: Look for the option that matches the main idea of the lesson.

questions.prompt: A signal repeats every 0.25 seconds. What is its frequency?
questions.hint: Write the relationship first, then substitute the values and keep the units.

units.title: Make a small device
units.description: Turn a circuit idea into a project plan.

lesson.heading: Test before you build
lesson.body: Start a circuit project by writing its intended behavior. Draw a block diagram, test each part, and keep notes about the results.
lesson.example: A simple indicator can be described as an input, a decision, and an output. Test each block before combining them.
lesson.activity: Write a short plan for a simulated indicator circuit. Describe its input and output.

questions.prompt: What helps locate a problem in a prototype?
questions.explanation: Testing parts separately helps locate where the behavior differs from the plan.
questions.hint: Look for the option that matches the main idea of the lesson.

questions.prompt: A device uses 2 W for 3 hours. How much energy does it use?
questions.explanation: Energy = power × time = 2 W × 3 h = 6 Wh.
questions.hint: Write the relationship first, then substitute the values and keep the units.

courses.title: Ideas & experiments
courses.description: A notebook for questions, prototypes, and useful mistakes.

units.title: Ask a better question
units.description: Turn curiosity into something you can investigate.

lesson.heading: Make it testable
lesson.body: A testable question names something you can change or observe. Narrow a broad idea into a small comparison with a clear outcome.
lesson.example: Instead of asking for the best design, ask which of two shapes spans a fixed gap with less deflection under the same load.
lesson.activity: Write a question you can investigate in one short session.

questions.prompt: Which question is easiest to test?
options: Which shape bends less under the same load?
questions.explanation: A defined comparison gives the experiment a measurable outcome.
questions.hint: Look for the option that matches the main idea of the lesson.

questions.prompt: You compare 2 designs with 3 trials each. How many trials do you run?
questions.explanation: 2 designs × 3 trials per design = 6 trials.
questions.hint: Write the relationship first, then substitute the values and keep the units.

units.title: Keep a useful notebook
units.description: Document the process while it is happening.

lesson.heading: Record the details
lesson.body: A notebook makes an experiment easier to understand and repeat. Record the setup, the measurements, and the choices you make.
lesson.example: Write observations separately from interpretations. “The strip bent 4 mm” is an observation; an explanation comes afterward.
lesson.activity: Write one observation and one possible interpretation of a simple experiment.
lesson.formula: total time = trials × time per trial

questions.prompt: Which is an observation?
questions.explanation: A measured displacement records what happened without assuming a cause.
questions.hint: Look for the option that matches the main idea of the lesson.

questions.prompt: Five trials take 2 minutes each. How long do they take in total?
questions.explanation: 5 × 2 = 10 minutes.
questions.hint: Write the relationship first, then substitute the values and keep the units.

units.title: Prototype the smallest version
units.description: Choose an experiment that answers one question.

lesson.heading: Build enough to learn
lesson.body: A first prototype needs to answer a question. Choose the simplest version that lets you observe the behavior you care about.
lesson.example: A paper model can test a layout before you build the final object. Decide what the model can show and what it cannot show.
lesson.activity: Describe a small prototype and the single question it will answer.

questions.prompt: What should a first prototype do?
questions.explanation: A focused prototype can help you learn before investing in a larger build.
questions.hint: Look for the option that matches the main idea of the lesson.

questions.prompt: A model uses one quarter of a 20 cm length. How long is it?
questions.hint: Write the relationship first, then substitute the values and keep the units.

units.title: Share what you learned
units.description: Explain the result and choose the next step.

lesson.heading: Tell the experiment’s story
lesson.body: A useful project summary connects the original question to the evidence. Explain the method, show the result, and name a limitation.
lesson.example: A result that differs from your expectation can still be useful. Describe what it rules out and what you would test next.
lesson.activity: Write a four-sentence summary: question, method, result, next step.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a project reflection?
questions.explanation: A limitation helps others understand what the evidence supports.
questions.hint: Look for the option that matches the main idea of the lesson.

questions.prompt: You have 8 observations and use 6 in a comparison. How many remain?
questions.explanation: 8 − 6 = 2 observations.
questions.hint: Write the relationship first, then substitute the values and keep the units.
